title: Finding a sangha
hookLine: temples, meditation centers, small groups: what to look for
last: A TIBETAN DAY — THE DIAMOND DAY.

lines: THE THIRD JEWEL IS A COMMUNITY.
cards: For more than three hundred days, a lot of this path has happened between you and a screen. Early mornings, a bell, a breath. That counts.
But the refuge itself makes a point about people.
Of the three jewels, the Buddha, the teaching and the community, one is other people: people who sit when you don't feel like it, people who notice when you've gone missing. Today: finding a sangha.

teach.b: Sangha first meant the community of monks and nuns. Today many people also use it for any group who practice together, and it comes in a few shapes. First, temples.
In many cities there are Thai, Sri Lankan, Vietnamese, Chinese, Korean, Japanese and Tibetan temples, built by communities who brought the teaching with them.
Many welcome visitors, and some offer meditation classes in English. You may be the only newcomer in the room, and someone may hand you a plate of food.
Second, meditation centers: insight, Zen, Tibetan, with a weekly sit, a talk, and sometimes retreats.
Third, small groups: a handful of people in a living room, a library, a church basement, or online, sitting together on a Tuesday night. What should you look for?
Teachers who are open about where their teaching comes from. Money that's explained; many groups run on dana, freely given. No pressure to commit, buy, or cut other ties.
Room to ask questions. And one simple test: after a while, do the people who've been there longest seem kinder, calmer, more honest? That's the fruit.

First visits are often awkward: you may not know when to bow, where to put your shoes, or what the chant is. That's normal. Try a place more than once before you decide, and it's fine to visit several.
This week brings the admirable friend, warning signs, visiting a temple, and taking refuge. It starts here.

how: Buddhists practice with a sangha at temples serving their communities, at meditation centers with weekly sits and retreats, and in small lay groups meeting in homes or online; many groups run on donations (dana).

join three other groups the same week.
games.why: first visits are often awkward. try a place more than once, and it's fine to visit several.

practice: Wonder, without needing an answer yet, where people near you gather to practice: a temple, a center, a small group, even one that meets online.
Then sit with the breath, and remember that somewhere, in a temple or a living room, others are sitting too.

wordCard.voice: Sangha. The community of practice: first the monastic order, now also any group, temple or circle where people sit together.

orig.note: Pali saṅgha: community, assembly; first the monastic order, now often any community of practitioners.

carryVoice: Your line: you need people. The third jewel is other people, and they're out there. Day three hundred nineteen.
